President Weed stated that he had received word from Edward T. Rich
ards, Sigma '27, Secretary of the Executive Council, to the effect that some of
the CJhapters had expressed a desire to have certain topics discussed on the
Convention floor, such topics including, among others, the matter of expansion,
the "blackball" system, and the possible authorization of Psi Upsilon rings.
Ronald A. Harbert, Phi '54, requested permission to address the Conven
tion. Recognition having been obtained, he stated that the Phi Chapter desired
te recommend that in the future all Chapter votes on a petition for a new

chapter should be treated as secret ballots. He further stated that any petition
ing group should be given considerable publicity in the Diamond before the
Chapters were required to cast votes on any petition received from such group.
He stated that the Phi believed that the vote of each Chapter should not be
made known until after all of the Chapters had voted, and that the Phi Chapter
felt that pressure had been brought to bear on the Phi Chapter te change its
vote on a petition.

Harold L. Field, Upsilon '10, a member of the Executive Council, explained
that the Executive Council did not divulge the results of any vote, and he ex
plained the position that had been taken by the Executive Council in connec
tion with the matter ef the petition of the Theta Epsilon. He stated that
the installation of a new chapter at the University ef Southern California had
been under consideration for some time, and that the Executive Council had
not brought any pressure to bear in the matter. It was observed that there was
no way, and should be no way, in which the votes of active Brothers on a
peti
tion of a group soliciting membership in Psi Upsilen could be controlled.

Henry N. Woolman, Tau '96, a member of the Executive Council, added
that he felt Psi Upsilen should be careful net to alienate the help of our alumni
in expanding the Fraternity.
The Recorder was requested, by the President, te read the Bylaws, with
regard to voting on the installation of a petitioning group. It was then recom
mended by the President, that the matter of petitions be referred to the Com
mittee on New Business, and that they in turn discuss the subject with the dele
gates from the Phi Chapter.

should be some instruction on the proper usage ef the system which, in and of

certain amount of paddling resulted in better discipline. President Weed re
marked that hazing smacked of adolescence. Brother Karl P. Harrington, Xi

Delta (Leon V. Murray, Jr., '52). AH the fratemities at New York Uni
versity are in a difficult situation due to the decreasing number ef out-of-city
students entering the University and the corresponding decrease in the regu
larly small nuraber of prospective fraternity raen.
Through well-organized and spirited rushing programs and the generous
financial support given by our alurani, the Delta has managed to maintain its
position of prominence and the respect and prestige of the faculty and studentbody.
During this past year the Chapter consisted of twenty-one men, of whom
nine were seniors graduating this June. Despite this low membership, the

Page Ten

Chapter had had a financially successful year and, again through alumni assist
ance, the House has continued to be the most attractive, inside and outside, of
all the houses on the campus.

Although the list of scholastic standings ef the fraternities for the past
year has net yet been compiled by the school, we are confident that the Chapter
has made an appreciable advance from its previous position of eleventh of
thirteen. For the past four or five years the large majority of the Brothers of the
Delta have been students in the College of Engineering; however, the house
average has consistently been within a few points of the academic leaders
whose members are largely Liberal Arts students.

Socially, the Delta is "the big House on campus". With our open-door
policy toward ether fraternities and particularly toward the faculty, the Chapter
has done much to increase the good reputation of Psi Upsilon on our campus
and te bring about closer relationship between Fraternity and University.

Similarly outstanding has been the Chapter's participation and success in
Inter-Fraternity athletics, having taken the football and softbaU trophies and
entering the finals in basketball and track. The past year has seen a greater
number of Delta men in varsity athletics than has been the case for many
years, with members on the varsity football, baseball, and rifle teams.
Even mere active has been the participation in non-athletic extra-curricular
activities, with men en the Student Council, the Editorial staff of the technical
publication, and in nearly every engineering society on the campus. For the
third ef the past four years the highest ranking cadet officer (Colonel) in the
R.O.T.C. has been a Psi U. Three ef our Brothers have distinguished themselves
by election to top honorary Engineering fraternities. In the annual "Fresh
Follies", a show put on by fraternities, clubs and other organizations on the
campus, the Chapter won another addition to its trophy mantel with the presen
tation of the best musical skit.
With plans for an all-out rushing program for the fall already underway,
the Delta leeks forward to another successful and creditable year as part ef the
great National Fratemity of Psi Upsilon.
Sigma

(Edmund D. Mooney, '53). For the Sigma, the year 1951-52 was an
eventful and difficult year of transition. At its outset, membership was at a very
low point, both because of the large graduating Senier delegation of the previ
ous year (16 Brothers) and because of the additional less ef 5 Brothers from
the lower delegations and the Pledge Qass who had taken leaves of absence te
join the Armed Forces. To add to the Chapter's difficulties, we had been
directed by the University to move out of our house at 4 Manning Street into
unfinished quarters in the new Brown Quadrangle. There we had to carefully
pick our way through tangles of dangling electric wires and piles of construc
tion debris. Also, we were forced to wait ever a month and a half for the com
pletion of our lounge facilities and ever five months for the completion of our
Chapter Room to a point where we could use it for formal meetings. Despite
the handicaps ef inadequate facilities and the distraction of construction activi
ties, however, Upper Class Rushing was conducted in the dormitory rooms and
we gained three pledges.

Realizing that the low membership caused an unusual need for dose inte
gration and efficient cooperation, the (Qiapter got down to brass tacks and pro

tion by our members. On the track team, two Brothers; the golf team, one
Brother; the NROTC rifle team, two Brothers; the ski team, one Brother
(David Bell, who is also Vice-President of the Ski Club) ; the soccer team, two
Brothers; the Yacht Club, six Brothers, including George McGowan, who is
Regatta Chairman; and the Chapel Choir, two Brothers. Parties at the Sigma
were, as usual, the best on the HiU.

of the
rushing. Our Pledge Class was somewhat stronger than last year's. Many

(Harry C. Rubicam '53). The Gamma Chapter completed a year
which saw the Brothers engaged in every activity on the T^herst campus. In

golf, and captains-elect in wrestling and tennis.
In the New England IntercoUegiates, Brothers McGrath and Schellenger
reached the finals in wrestling, the latter taking the 130-pound crown. The
touch football team won the intramural championship, and all House teams
throughout the year met with better-than-average success, the Heuse placing
fourth out of fourteen in the overall standings.
Scholastically the Chapter's record was somewhat checkered. We lost four
Brothers from our sophomore delegation at midyears, which caused the House
to drop to twelfth position in scholastic ratings. However, the scholarship com
mittee has been rejuvenated and is receiving the active co-operation of all the
Brothers, which would seem to indicate that our present position is merely a
temporary one.
The Chapter, with the help of several graduate brothers, exerted its influ
ence to aid the administration in a campus-wide de-emphasis of social life. The
need for this de-emphasis was brought about primarily by the central location
of the college and its traditional hospitality.
However, despite restrictions on the serving of liquor in the House, the
